newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS - Singapore dollar caves in to regional woes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Singapore dollar caves in to regional woes.

text.p: The Singapore dollar slid to 32-month lows against the U.S. dollar on Thursday and will remain hostage to the fortunes of its neighbours and the U.S. dollar's overall strength in the near term, analysts said.
The Singapore dollar fell through the psychological support level of 1.47 to the U.S. dollar on early stop-loss sales, diving to levels not seen since November 1994.
It banged down to a low of 1.4785 and was quoted around 1.4770/80 at 0830 GMT. On July 10, it was selling for 1.4305 to the U.S. dollar.

Foreign exchange dealers attributed Thursday's selling spree to Finance Minister Richard Hu's comments about Singapore's competitiveness not being hurt by the tumble of other Southeast Asian currencies in recent weeks.
Hu told parliament on Wednesday Singapore's exchange rate was determined by market demand and it would continue to be managed on a trade-weighted basis with a medium-term perspective.

With other Southeast Asian currencies continuing to feel the heat from the de facto devaluations of the Thai baht and Philippine peso earlier this month, dealers and economists said the Singapore dollar was likely to fall further.

"The 1.48 level has always been a psychological resistance (for the U.S. dollar). But over the medium term, 1.50 is definitely in the pipeline with most market players," a sales desk manager at a U.S. bank said.
Analysts said such weakness would not be out of line with the Singapore government's exchange rate policy, especially in view of the U.S. dollar's recent bull run against the mark.

"Given that many of Singapore's trading partners' currencies are weakening, if you're faithful to the basket then you're going to go down against the U.S. dollar, which is gaining virtually against every currency in the world," said Christopher Chong, head of research at HSBC James Capel.
He said the Singapore dollar was being driven in part by the fact that the U.S. dollar, yen and Malaysian ringgit were major elements in Singapore's trade-weighted basket.

Desmond Supple, head of Asian currency research at BZW Asia, said weakness in Asian currencies was no longer being driven merely by speculative flows as investors were increasingly reassessing the region's risk-reward valuations.

"There's no reason to believe the Singapore dollar would be immune to that reassessment, though fundamentally the currency is far less vulnerable to short-term outflows due to Singapore's impressive current account position," Supple said.
Singapore has foreign exchange reserves of around Singapore $115 billion.
Supple said the Singapore dollar might need to weaken towards 1.50 to the U.S. dollar to guard against overvaluation of the currency if the region's woes worsened.
"The Singapore dollar is still strong on a trade-weighted basis, so there's no substantial risk to imported inflation," he added.
Analysts said the baht, which has dropped 21.5 percent against the U.S. dollar this year, was likely to hold the key to the fortunes of regional currencies.
"I would expect the Singapore dollar to end the year around 1.4350. The only intangible is what happens to the Thai baht," said P.K. Basu, economist at UBS Singapore.
"A lot depends on how quickly Thailand can arrange either a consortium of lenders or a loan from the IMF (International Monetary Fund) to plug the gap in its current account," he said.
